channel.title: Stanford HAI News
channel.description: AI research, policy, and societal impact news from Stanford HAI

item.title: AI-Enabled Video System Monitors ICU Patients for Early Signs of Delirium
item.description: Computer vision experts have developed a 24/7 video monitoring system that tracks patient activity and helps doctors identify subtle signs of delirium.

item.title: AI Might Be Flooding State Court Houses, but Proving It Is Another Matter
item.description: Stanford researchers use a novel benchmark built from documented AI hallucination cases to calibrate detectors and track generative AI’s rise across four U.S. state courts.

item.title: AI’s Future Is Still a Choice
item.description: At Stanford HAI’s fall conference, experts explored how decisions about governance, work, and education can turn AI’s promise into broader public benefit.

item.title: Stanford HAI Backs Ambitious AI Projects with 2026 Hoffman-Yee Grants
item.description: Seven interdisciplinary research teams win a total of $3.5 million to pursue bold human-centered approaches to AI across medicine, science, law and education.

item.title: The Jagged Edge of the AI Boom
item.description: New findings from the Stanford AI Index reveal a more uneven picture of public sentiment and labor market outcomes than previously thought, as AI investment surpasses $1 trillion.

item.title: Research Teams Mine the Intersection of Neuroscience and AI
item.description: Wu Tsai Neuro and HAI are again teaming up to support efforts to better treat psychiatric disease, understand brain development, and improve AI models with inspiration from human experience.

item.title: The World Has Changed: Insights From The New AI100 Report
item.description: From battlefield targeting to synthetic media, the third AI100 report finds a technology that has outrun both expectations and governance.

item.title: Tracking AI’s Real-Time Footprint On The Labor Market
item.description: Dashboards created by Stanford HAI’s Digital Economy Lab measure how AI adoption is altering employment trends and job growth, along with broader economic indicators.

item.title: Measuring What Medical AI Can Actually Do
item.description: Over three years, we’ve built progressively harder, more realistic benchmarks for medical AI. Here’s what we learned.

item.title: Who is Responsible When AI Causes Harm?
item.description: It's one of AI policy's hardest unsolved problems. Expert Deb Raji joins Stanford HAI to find answers that move beyond principles and into practice.

item.title: Humans and AI Engage in Meaningful Collaborations
item.description: Analyzing thousands of human-AI conversations, a new study shows that people are turning to chatbots for increasingly critical tasks – and that productive outcomes depend on how the collaboration unfolds.

item.title: Want Employees to Embrace AI? Stop Selling It as a Productivity Tool
item.description: How managers introduce and support AI determines whether workers engage with or resist the technology.

item.title: Stanford HAI Welcomes 15 New HAI Data Science Scholars
item.description: The two-year fellowship supports PhD researchers across law, medicine, physics, statistics, education, and engineering.

item.title: The Tests That Grade AI May Be Getting It Wrong
item.description: Benchmarks — the standardized tests that rank AI models on safety, bias, and reasoning — drive markets and shape regulation. New Stanford research finds they often don't measure what they claim to.

item.title: Can AI Be Slowed Down? Stanford HAI Experts Weigh the Risks, Rules and Race Ahead
item.description: In a new series called Prompt Response, Stanford’s Surya Ganguli, Diyi Yang and Rob Reich examined emergent agent behavior, recursive self-improvement, independent evaluation and whether a kill switch can make advanced AI safer.

item.title: AI Legal Review Says Millions Live Under Discriminatory Local Laws
item.description: Building an AI pipeline to comb through millions of local statutes, researchers at Stanford Law School turn a spotlight on unsavory laws still on the books in communities across the country.

item.title: Your ‘For You’ Algorithm Disagrees With You
item.description: A new Stanford-led study finds that X’s “For You” algorithm mistakes outrage for interest – and fills your feed accordingly.

item.title: Companies That Buy and Sell Your Data Are Not Following California’s Strict Privacy Laws
item.description: A new Stanford study shows data brokers are making it difficult for consumers to submit privacy requests and failing to report how many privacy requests they receive.
